LGBTQIA+ Inclusion Training Program in India by ASK Insights

ASK Insights runs an LGBTQIA+ inclusion training program in India built and delivered with consultants from the LGBTQIA+ community itself, not generalist trainers reading from a shared deck. The sessions combine real experience with scenario based practice, so participants leave with more than an awareness certificate.

Discuss LGBTQIA+ Inclusion Training for Your Organization

What Is ASK Insights’ LGBTQIA+ Program?

ASK Insights’ LGBTQIA+ program is a sensitization and inclusion session built for every level of an organization, from new hires to the CEO’s own leadership team. It sits inside the company’s wider Developmental Journeys work alongside the Women Leadership, Gender Intelligence, and Disability Positive tracks, and focuses specifically on breaking down outdated assumptions about the LGBTQIA+ experience at work.

The distinguishing choice is who delivers it. Most corporate LGBTQIA+ training in India is run by generalist DEI facilitators who have studied the subject. ASK Insights instead partners with consultants from the LGBTQIA+ community to lead sessions, so the material comes from lived experience instead of secondhand research.

LGBTQIA+ Inclusion Training Program in India: What Makes the Approach Different?

Three choices separate this from a standard one hour sensitization deck.

Real Voices, Not Generic Scripts

Sessions are co-led by LGBTQIA+ community consultants who share personal experience alongside the training content, instead of a facilitator presenting the community’s experience secondhand.

Scenario Based, Not Lecture Based

Participants work through real workplace situations, an uncomfortable comment in a meeting, a colleague coming out, a hiring decision, instead of sitting through a straight lecture on terminology. The goal is practical empathy that holds up outside the training room, not just inside it.

A Safe Space That Is Actually Built, Not Just Named

Facilitators are trained to keep the room genuinely judgment free, so participants can ask an honest question or admit a bias without it becoming a disciplinary moment. Programs that skip this step tend to get performative answers instead of real ones.

Why This Matters in India?

India’s legal landscape around LGBTQIA+ rights has moved quickly. The Supreme Court read down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code in 2018, decriminalizing consensual same sex relationships, following its 2014 NALSA judgment recognizing transgender persons’ right to self identify their gender. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 went further for employers specifically: it prohibits discrimination against transgender employees in recruitment, promotion, and other employment matters, and requires every establishment to publish an Equal Opportunity Policy for transgender persons and designate a complaint officer to handle violations.

Most Indian companies have not caught up to what the law already requires, let alone what genuine inclusion looks like day to day. That gap between legal compliance and lived experience at work is exactly where ASK Insights’ program is built to operate. Publishing a policy document satisfies the letter of the Transgender Persons Act. It does nothing on its own to change how a manager reacts when an employee comes out, or whether a colleague feels safe using the name and pronouns they have asked for. That is the layer training has to reach, and policy alone cannot.

Proof in the Field

At Reckitt, LGBTQIA+ sensitization was rolled out to the entire population of people managers at the company’s Global Hub, delivered alongside a broader inclusion push that covered more than 3,000 training hours and reached 80 percent of employees in a single year. At ABB, LGBTQIA+ focused equal opportunity commitments were built into a wider DEI programme that ran alongside the company’s unconscious bias and allyship training, part of the work that later won ABB a Times of India and Ask Insights DEI Award. Neither engagement was a single afternoon session. Both sat inside a multi-year DEI relationship, which is consistent with how ASK Insights builds every track in its Developmental Journeys work, as a sustained program rather than a one-time booking.

Who This Program Is Built For?

The session is designed for two audiences at once. All employees, from a new hire to the CEO, go through the same material, since everyone in an organization has some role in creating an inclusive space. Managers and leaders get additional focus on building and running teams where an LGBTQIA+ colleague can actually thrive, not just avoid being singled out. Organizations that have run a single generic diversity workshop and seen no real change in how comfortable LGBTQIA+ employees feel tend to be the ones that get the most out of this specific program. It also suits organizations specifically working through the requirements of the Transgender Persons Act, since the training gives managers the practical skills a compliance policy cannot provide on its own.

The Expertise Behind the Program

Dr. Niru Kumar, MBBS, Founder and CEO of ASK Insights and a Padma Shri recipient, and Dr. Akshay Kumar, who holds a PhD in Clinical and Positive Psychology and lectures at London Business School, oversee the program’s design and its integration into ASK Insights’ wider Developmental Journeys work. Delivery itself sits with consultants from the LGBTQIA+ community, which is a deliberate structural choice: expertise in organizational psychology sets the framework, and lived experience fills it in. That division of labour is intentional. A clinical psychologist can design a curriculum around bias and behaviour change, but only someone who has actually navigated being LGBTQIA+ at work can answer the specific, sometimes uncomfortable questions a room full of managers will ask.

Effective programs go beyond definitions into scenario-based practice and are often delivered with input from LGBTQIA+ community members themselves.

The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 prohibits employment discrimination against transgender persons and requires every establishment to publish an Equal Opportunity Policy and designate a complaint officer. There is no equivalent standalone statute covering sexual orientation, though the 2018 reading down of Section 377 removed the criminal law barrier to LGBTQIA+ inclusion more broadly.
